title: Village Board Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter Village Board held its August 24, 2026 regular meeting, covering a range of financial and operational matters including a 10-year capital improvement plan presentation, TID #1 valuation challenges, and a collective bargaining negotiation update. The board convened into closed session to address a police union contract and directed the administrator to continue negotiations before adjourning.

discussions.body: One speaker, Mr. Cramer, addressed the board regarding a previous special meeting where a trustee took over the chairmanship, calling it unusual and raising accountability concerns. He also cited the village attorney's budget memo noting the village is $1,000 over budget after seven months due to personnel investigation costs, and criticized the ongoing investigation timeline as several months with no public answers, stating 'I think you have a major accountability problem.'

The administrator reported on a meeting with the Golden Pond HOA regarding pond level management, noting the village found seven homes still running sump pumps when the HOA claimed only two, and that the village declined to raise the pond level as a result. The administrator also flagged a significant increase in open records requests targeting the police department, particularly records from when Village President Joling was police chief, characterizing them as a personal vendetta. Staff discussed potentially charging for staff time associated with open records requests and updating public comment procedures.

Public Works Director Greg reported that a WPS transformer installed for a new electrical panel was the wrong wattage, causing a delay of a few days on Lift Station 2. He also noted that a road contractor is working on drainage and shoulder improvements near the municipal building and bridge areas. A generator battery failure was discovered and addressed in-house, with discussion about the aging generator fleet and the need for a long-term replacement plan.

discussions.item: Finance Director Report - General Fund and TID #1
discussions.body: Finance Director John Jacobs reported the general fund revenues are tracking nearly identically to 2025 at about 62.7% collected through seven months, with most remaining revenue expected from the state in October. Three expenditure areas flagged as over budget - legal/investigation costs, municipal building operations, and garbage/recycling - are expected to be addressed via a transfer from the $60,000 contingency reserve later in the year. On TID #1, Jacobs explained a combined $2.5 million valuation reduction resulted from local assessor adjustments and a retroactive state correction, worsening the TID's cash flow. He recommended a status quo approach for six to nine months to allow a potential distribution center project to add tax increment, noting debt payments drop significantly starting in 2030 and TID #1 debt is eliminated by 2037-2044.

Finance Director Jacobs and Public Works Director Greg presented the 10-year CIP, noting the village currently has roughly $49 million in remaining borrowing capacity at 70% of the debt limit. The first-year 2027 program totals approximately $4.3 million across equipment, infrastructure, parks, and facilities. Trustee Erin Mishka (Parks Committee Chair) specifically noted that the $200,000 in park donations listed for 2027 is insufficient and that tax dollars should support parks improvements. Staff noted a potential $1.7 million general obligation borrowing target and discussed strategic timing of debt issuance to defer tax impact. No formal vote was taken; the presentation was informational ahead of the fall budget process.

Administrator Jim reported that the developer of the Green Tree subdivision indicated they expect to move forward within the next month and wants board action. The Plan Commission made a conditional recommendation in June, and staff noted some ordinance timing provisions require the board to act before the approval becomes automatic. A related factor is a pending decision regarding the golf course that may affect the subdivision layout. No vote was taken; the board noted this will return as a formal agenda item.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Seclusion Room at Evergreen Elementary
discussions.body: Mary Soulheim, a district resident and parent of students at Evergreen Elementary, addressed the board about behavioral intervention practices. She stated the district was found in direct violation of Wisconsin Statute 118.305 for maintaining a seclusion room with a locked door and hazards at Evergreen Elementary during the 2024-2025 school year. She described the room as a former storage closet measuring just over 4 by 6 feet, and argued that retrofitting it with padding and training staff to use it for seclusion would be traumatizing to students and shift school culture away from proactive mental health support. She urged the board to halt the rollout of the plan and direct administration to conduct a review of legal and psychological risks, proposing the topic be brought back in September.

discussions.body: Larry Schaefer reported on the CISA 9 annual meeting, noting that Gary Moon from North Lakeland was elected as the large-district representative, ending Schaefer's tenure on the CISA 9 Board of Control after four years. Board President Shannon Grabko read aloud a commendation letter from CISA 9 administrator Al Betri praising Schaefer's service, leadership, and professionalism. Schaefer encouraged any board member interested in attending future CISA 9 annual meetings or serving on the board of control to do so, describing it as a valuable perspective on upcoming educational issues.

discussions.body: Superintendent Dr. Knight reported that the community survey on the facility study is being finalized, with staff receiving it September 14 and community members receiving it by USPS the week of September 21; a board workshop to review results is expected in November. Officer Matt Loveless described a four-day joint critical incident rescue task force training held at the middle school July 27-30, involving approximately 30 Mountain Bay Metro Police officers and 20 Riverside Fire District personnel, using student volunteers for realistic scenarios. Dr. Knight also reported that after a demo, the district decided not to implement a $4,000 AI chatbot from Final Site this year due to cost, quality concerns, and pending ADA compliance rules effective April 2026.

Mike Rayther and Nikki Matthews presented the summer learning report in Rayther's first year leading the program. Highlights included an Engineering Tomorrow partnership with Greenheck on sound mitigation, strength and conditioning programming with CTI, a patriotic musical performance called 'America 250' involving about 70 students, the Hmong enrichment program co-run with Wausau School District and CESA, new courses including podcasting, sign language ('Flying Fingers'), and an art course for first and second graders, and the Fuel for the Weekend food program serving 127 families. Board members praised the program and asked about challenges and staff retention; Rayther said returning staff significantly outnumbered new staff this summer.

Dr. Strike presented the annual 10-year capital plan, noting it is required because the district holds a Fund 46 capital trust fund. She highlighted that some items are marked 'hold for facility study' pending the outcome of the ongoing facility planning process, and that furniture replacement has become an increasing need. The board approved the plan without discussion.

Dr. Strike presented the updated employee handbook for the upcoming school year, noting five themes of changes compiled by the talent and culture department, including Christy Eser and Sarah Trimmer. She noted most changes had been previously presented to the board earlier in the year and were being formalized through the handbook process. The board approved the handbook without discussion.

title: Administrative Policy Committee Meeting
overview: The Village of Kronenwetter's Administrative Policy Committee met on August 18, 2026, with Finance Director John leading the majority of discussions focused on the upcoming property reassessment, 2026 equalized valuation data, existing debt obligations, and the newly drafted 2027-2036 Capital Improvement Program. The meeting was significant for residents as officials revealed the village is approximately 40% below required full market value assessment, that TID 1 faces serious financial pressure if the anticipated distribution center development does not proceed this fall, and that opportunities exist in 2029-2030 for strategic debt-financed infrastructure investment.

discussions.body: Trustee Mary Solheim moved to approve the June 15th meeting minutes as presented, seconded by Misty Swanson. The motion passed 4-0 with no discussion.

Finance Director John reported that the exterior reassessment will begin the week of August 24th, with five assessors working in the field. He explained the village is approximately 40% below required full market value and faces a state takeover of the reassessment — at two to three times the cost — if not completed by end of 2027. The reassessment is being funded through budget surpluses from prior years when positions were unfilled, avoiding any new budget line item. Trustee Guy Fridale raised concerns about negative social media commentary and suggested early, repeated public messaging that the village only controls its portion of the tax levy. John noted that no valuation changes will appear on the December 2026 tax bill and that some property owners seeing a below-average valuation increase could actually see a tax reduction. The committee also discussed reviewing potentially tax-exempt parcels that may no longer qualify.

discussions.item: 2026 Preliminary Equalized Valuation and TID Increments
discussions.body: John reported that the village's equalized valuation rose by approximately $101 million in 2026, nearly a 10% increase, now exceeding $1.2 billion, but that assessed valuation remains around $700 million — only about 63% of full market value. Net new construction came in at just 0.65% for the third consecutive year, limiting the village's allowable tax levy increase without an exception to approximately $12,000. TID 1 was identified as the village's most significant financial concern: a 12% drop in valuation from $21 million to $19 million resulted from assessor adjustments on two parcels near Kowalski and Highway 39, compounded by a state-issued prior year correction of $1.4 million. John emphasized that if the anticipated distribution center in TID 1 does not break ground this fall, the village could face a shortfall of $1.5 million or more by 2044, potentially depleting the general fund reserve built over recent years. Fridale observed that TIDs 2 and 4 are performing well and noted TID 3 closed in February.

John reported that after seven months (58% of the year), the general fund had collected approximately 62% of budgeted revenues and spent about 49% of budgeted expenditures, indicating a healthy position. He cautioned that public works billing typically lags field work and that costs will increase. Three ongoing budget concerns — village attorney fees, municipal building costs, and garbage — remain unresolved. John acknowledged the 2025 audit has not yet been completed due to competing priorities including the reassessment launch and 2027 budget preparation, but expressed confidence that the audit could be finalized in time for the October budget workshops. Committee members praised John's work stabilizing village finances and noted the village operates with limited finance staff.

discussions.item: Review of Existing Debt Obligations Outstanding
discussions.body: John reviewed all outstanding debt, totaling approximately $14.5 million, of which $10 million is general obligation debt — representing only 17% of the village's $59 million maximum borrowing capacity. He identified the 2016 TID 1 redevelopment lease revenue bonds as a wait-and-see situation given low interest rates of 2.45-3.2% and the pending distribution center development. The 2024 general obligation bonds at 4-5% interest were flagged as a future refinancing candidate once callable in April 2029. He highlighted that debt service tax levy obligations drop significantly in 2029 (by ~$226,000) and 2030 (by ~$165,000), creating an opportunity window for infrastructure investment. Fridale and others emphasized the importance of TID 2 and TID 4 closure timelines — estimated around 2032 and 2033 respectively — as additional fiscal opportunities.

John and Public Works Director Greg presented the village's first-ever 10-year Capital Improvement Program, drafted using dedicated CIP software rather than Excel to improve accuracy and fluidity. The draft CIP covers projects across fire, municipal center, parks, police, public works, sewer, and water utilities, with a preliminary 2027 total of approximately $4.3 million. Funding sources include approximately $1.2 million in unused TID 2 bond proceeds that must be redirected if not spent on a TID project by October 2027, potential borrowing, utility depreciation funds, and donations. John noted the parks committee provided additional input the prior evening and that figures will be updated before the September presentation. The committee discussed potential borrowing scenarios — ranging from $1 million to $10 million — and agreed that a formal affordability analysis presenting multiple options would be prepared for the September APC meeting and budget workshops. No final decisions were made.

The committee used a card-sorting exercise to identify park improvement priorities and tentatively mapped projects across fiscal years 2027–2036, with Bushka Park playground replacement as the top priority for 2027.

discussions.body: Dan moved to approve the previous meeting minutes as presented; Patty seconded. No discussion followed. The motion passed unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Village Communications About Parks Within the Community
discussions.body: The committee reviewed the village website's park content, noting Jennifer had added videos in 2023 that were well-received. Members suggested promoting park videos on social media, adding short trail-walking videos, and including a notice in the village newsletter directing residents to check out park resources. Greg noted that once the Chromter Drive project wraps up, the village plans to add wayfinding signs near apartments directing people to trails at the municipal center.

The committee conducted a card-sorting exercise where each member wrote capital improvement ideas on cards, which were then grouped by park to identify priorities. The top vote-getter was the Bushka Park playground replacement (five or more cards), followed by Friendship/Cercas Park rubber surfacing replacement (estimated $70,000–$80,000), Towering Pines Park shelter and restroom development (proposed as a multi-year civic-style park project), and the municipal center park (restroom and potential disc golf course, estimated $150,000+). The committee tentatively assigned Bushka Park playground for 2027, Friendship Park surfacing for 2029, Towering Pines for 2030–2032, and municipal center park for 2033. General park signage, ADA improvements, and branding were discussed as ongoing priorities, with 2030 floated as an 'ADA year.' Civil Park new playground was placed at the end of the plan, approximately 2036–2037. Greg noted approximately $20,000 remains in a parks fund that could be directed toward near-term improvements such as a trail connecting Friendship Park to the dog park.

Erin Mishka reported $1,000 in sponsorships secured with a goal of $1,225 to fund participant shirts; no registration fee is charged and donations are voluntary. Chief [Cherry McHugh] approved a list of priority intersections for volunteer safety coverage, and committee members offered to staff intersections wearing high-visibility vests. The route was adjusted from the original plan so both the 3K and 5K now start and end at Bushka Park. Relocation (a local business) is hosting a raffle and 50/50 drawing, with the 50/50 beginning the week prior. Water stations will be set up at Bushka Park and civil park (halfway point), with Jennifer volunteering to cover water costs. Start time is 10 a.m. on a Saturday.

discussions.item: Future Fundraising Ideas — Living River Concert
discussions.body: Erin Mishka announced plans for a Living River Concert in May, with $1,000 in sponsorship already secured and an anonymous donor covering the band cost, resulting in no cost to the village. She proposed holding the event at Towering Pines and directing proceeds to the Bushka Park Fund Reserve. A committee member (Tim) raised a constituent concern about why residents must fundraise for parks rather than relying on tax dollars; other members acknowledged the concern but noted the village board has been supportive, including a $5,000 match on a recent grant. A running total of approximately $16,000 raised for Bushka Park was referenced.

Members identified several non-capital quick fixes for parks crew attention: removing no-dog signs, repairing a broken plexiglass circle on old wooden playground equipment at Bushka, adding paper towel holders in restrooms, installing at least one handicap swing, adding a bike rack on the farmers market side of Bushka Park, refreshing old wooden park signs at Nor-a-Plaza, Friendship, and Gooding parks, adding sand and a net to the Savil Park volleyball court, and investigating bike route signage connectivity with Rothschild. Greg noted the parks crew has been pressure-washing slides, shelters, and equipment during the slow grass-cutting period.

The committee discussed transitioning from bi-weekly to monthly or as-needed meetings, noting that Dan's return to teaching makes the 4 p.m. time slot difficult. After discussion, the group tentatively agreed to meet Tuesday, September 8 (pending confirmation that a quorum can attend), at 4:30 p.m., with the primary focus of reviewing CIP dollar amounts to present to the village board and finalizing 5K run details.

discussions.body: Six residents spoke during public comment. Jim Pensol encouraged civic engagement and described how public turnout once reversed a board decision to rename Schofield Avenue to DC Everest Boulevard. Kyra Lenzo addressed the animal fancier licensing issue, defending her care of four huskies and offering to expand her fenced outdoor space to comply with any space requirements. A neighbor, identified as a Borcart family member at 604 North Lane, complained about waste runoff from Lenzo's dogs onto their property citing ordinance sections 10.12, 10.19, and 10.29. Scott Borcart (County Road H) and Tony Hase (Danny's Girls vendor) both urged the board to keep the farmers market at Kennedy Park, with Hase noting business had improved significantly since the Alderson roundabout opened. Steve Mel spoke on the rezoning item (agenda item 43), arguing the planning commission's denial was improperly influenced by planner Jennifer Higgins's personal preference against storage facilities and citing Wisconsin Act 67's limitations on CUP denials.

discussions.item: Joint Resolution 2026-0001: Mountain Bay Metro PD Headquarters Debt Authorization
discussions.body: Trustee Ermeling raised significant concerns about the repayment structure, noting that at $130,000 per year minimum, it could take approximately 34-40 years for Mountain Bay Metro PD to fully repay the municipalities for the construction loan, while Weston would need to increase its levy by roughly $206,000 annually to service the 20-year debt. Village Administrator and police representatives clarified that $130,000 is a minimum and that the Oversight Board can direct additional fund balance payments to accelerate repayment, with a goal of $250,000-$275,000 annually total from both municipalities. Ermeling and another trustee (believed to be Kern) voted no; the resolution passed 3-2. The agreement had been reviewed by Rothschild's financial advisors and Mountain Bay Metro's attorney but not Weston's own attorney, which Ermeling flagged as a concern for a multi-million-dollar commitment.

discussions.item: Farmers Market Location at Kennedy Park
discussions.body: The board voted 4-1 to continue the farmers market at Kennedy Park, with Trustee Ermeling casting the lone dissenting vote, expressing concern that the park's green space was being consumed. Trustee Olson outlined several proposed mitigation measures including enhanced parking enforcement, coning off intersections 15 feet in each direction, and reaching out to a neighboring property owner about sight-obscuring vegetation. Trustee Lopes-Serrao argued the market pays for itself, serves as a community gathering event, and that no viable alternative location exists. Village President Maloney said he has visited the market at least ten times and found it a positive experience. A suggestion to survey vendors and customers again after the Alderson roundabout opened was raised by Ermeling and supported by others as a future step.

discussions.item: Municipal Center Rooms as Public Meeting/Gathering Spaces
discussions.body: The board discussed but took no action on a proposal to open municipal center meeting rooms to the public for gatherings, a topic raised at a prior community engagement session. Multiple trustees and staff expressed opposition based on past experience with damage, cleaning costs, and supervision burdens — Clerk Pam described specific problems from her time at Schofield Township, including vandalism and post-party cleanup that exceeded security deposits. Trustee Olson said he was not firmly opposed but would not support it without an alternative to requiring staff supervision on weekends. No action was taken.

discussions.item: Rezoning Request: 4205 & 4307 Weston Avenue (B2 to LI) — Storage Facility
discussions.body: Trustee Lopes-Serrao moved to accept the Planning Commission's recommendation of denial for the rezoning of 4205 and 4307 Weston Avenue from B2 Highway Business to LI Limited Industrial for a proposed personal storage unit facility. A procedural issue was raised: overturning the planning commission's denial requires a 2/3 supermajority (five of seven votes), but with only five trustees present, all five would need to vote in favor of rezoning — effectively requiring unanimity to override. The motion to accept the denial received a second, and the transcript ends before the vote is recorded.

The Finance and HR Committee brought three preliminary priorities to the full board: one robotic mower pilot, a new facilities and grounds maintenance position, and three SAFER grant-funded fire/EMS staff positions phased in over 2027. Trustees discussed broadening the scope to include public safety (EMS, fire, police), drinking water infrastructure, code enforcement, and cybersecurity. Trustee Beck emphasized multi-year budget planning similar to the CIP process used in public works. A recent village comprehensive plan survey was cited showing road maintenance and EMS tied as top community priorities. No formal action was taken; further discussion is scheduled for a budget session on the 24th at 5:30.

The ordinance establishing a 30-day storage and disposal procedure for property removed during nuisance abatement was approved unanimously with brief discussion. Trustees agreed the 30-day window was reasonable to give property owners time to retrieve belongings.

The amendment to Section 10.123, which shifts animal fancier hearings from the Planning Commission to the Eclipse body, was approved unanimously after brief clarification that this item was about the procedural change, not the specific Lenzo dog license case addressed in public comment.

overview: The Kronenwetter Village Board held its August 10, 2026 meeting with six of seven trustees present (Stowell absent/excused). The board approved two significant actions: eliminating the village's oak wilt ordinance and reimbursement policy, and passing a one-year moratorium on new data center development applications to allow planning and utility committees time to study the issue. The meeting also featured extensive financial updates on the village's tax increment districts, equalization values, and upcoming property reassessment process.

discussions.body: Two written public comments were read into the record. Lamont Yager of Civil Road submitted a lengthy letter requesting enforcement of oak wilt ordinance 389-1 against the owner of 1916 Civil Road, asking police enforcement of 389-2 regarding a dead tree defined as a nuisance, and calling for an investigation of Village President Joling for alleged obstruction of justice, accusing him of being 'petty, tyrannical and vindictive.' President Joling noted that the tree in question is being handled following administrator Deval's contact with the property owner, who is waiting until after August 15th to cut the oak. A second letter was entered into the minutes without being read aloud due to length.

The police chief (referred to as 'Terry') reported on several notable incidents: a high number of domestic violence calls in July including one involving ten felony charges and three misdemeanors with a weapon; a 12-year sentence handed down in the Maple Ridge Road aggravated battery case, with the department receiving praise from the district attorney; and a high-speed pursuit of an attempted homicide suspect that came through Kronenwetter at speeds exceeding 120 mph, with KPD participating under their pursuit policy. Trustee Coyle asked about body camera status; the chief confirmed the department has had body cams since approximately 2021-2022, currently using updated units compatible with their in-car systems, with storage through City-County IT rather than higher-cost providers like Axon.

Administrator Deval welcomed new Community Development Director Nathan Samot, who began the previous Thursday. He updated the board on several matters: the Wausau School District superintendent plans to attend the October 12th board meeting to discuss a possible referendum; a meeting is planned with Green Tree regarding the Mortensen International Golf Course area and access issues; a lawsuit by St. Teresa Church over an open pit sand mine decision is pending a new judge after the original recused herself, with the village's attorney suggesting it may be thrown out; and an Act 10 update was referenced with no immediate action planned. Deval also noted that TID 1's prospective distribution center tenant may begin construction as early as September or October.

The administrator presented on behalf of the assessor, explaining that letters are being mailed today to all property owners informing them of an upcoming exterior revaluation process beginning the week of August 24th. A field team of five individuals from Associated Appraisal will survey the entire village. Property owners need take no action; the revaluation will affect December 2027 tax bills, not 2026. Assessment values are expected to need to increase on average approximately 40% to reach full value, as the current assessment ratio has fallen to 63%. The village must complete this revaluation by end of 2027 or the state will conduct it at two to three times the cost in 2028.

Finance Director John presented preliminary 2027 budget figures from the state. The village's equalized valuation reached nearly $1.2 billion, a $100 million or 9.4% increase, but only $8.8 million is net new construction, meaning the assessment ratio dropped from 69% to 63%. The net new construction limit means the tax levy can technically only increase by about $12,000 for 2027, which does not cover staff raises or basic costs. TID 1 saw a concerning $2.5 million valuation reduction — partly from the local assessor's obsolescence adjustments on two parcels and partly from an unexplained $1.4 million state correction the finance director is still awaiting explanation on — meaning the general fund advance to TID 1 could rise from roughly $125,000 to as much as $200,000 in 2027. On a positive note, the village has $49 million remaining under its general obligation debt limit and still has room under the 12% TID valuation cap, with the finance director flagging a potential future TID 5 to help finance a new water tower.

discussions.item: Consent Agenda - July 27, 2026 Village Board Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: Trustee Coyle moved and Trustee Mortensen seconded approval of the July 27, 2026 meeting minutes. The motion passed unanimously with no discussion.

The board discussed eliminating the village's oak wilt ordinance (389-1) and its associated reimbursement policy, following a unanimous recommendation from the CLIP committee on August 3rd. Key reasons cited included: the reimbursement fund has been depleted for several years, the village has no certified tree inspector on staff or under contract, and oak wilt is so prevalent throughout the village and surrounding municipalities that enforcement is not feasible. Trustee Solheim raised concern about losing the April-through-August pruning restriction window and its value for developers; staff noted the DNR classifies Marathon County in the north zone with a shorter April 15–July 15 restriction. The board agreed that DNR guidelines would be linked on the village website. Trustee Coyle moved and a trustee seconded to eliminate both the ordinance and reimbursement policy; the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-011 - Temporary Moratorium on New Data Center Development
discussions.body: The board considered a one-year moratorium on new data center development applications, referring the matter to the planning commission and utility committee for study of zoning, utility, infrastructure, and land use implications. Administrator Deval noted there is significant misinformation circulating about data centers and the village simply needs better information before acting on any application. Nathan Samot flagged a minor typographical error in the resolution. Trustee Coyle moved and Trustee Mortensen seconded; the resolution passed 7-0 on a roll call vote. It was noted that Marathon County is considering similar action covering townships, and each municipality must pass its own.

discussions.item: Public Comment: Rib Mountain Elementary Class Size
discussions.body: Two speakers addressed class size concerns at Rib Mountain Elementary. Ann Wicklund, a retired Wausau School District director of special education with 50 years in early childhood education, spoke about the developmental importance of K-3 class sizes and the risks of a projected 25-student first grade class, but was cut off slightly over her 3-minute limit. Nate Bartsch, a Rib Mountain parent speaking on behalf of many families present in the audience, argued that as a single-section school Rib Mountain has 'zero flexibility' to balance behavioral or academic needs across classrooms, and asked the board for immediate action for the 2026-27 school year rather than just acknowledgment.

Board President Bouché sought a motion to approve the consent agenda covering staff appointments, replacements, contract changes, separations, leaves, retirements, meeting minutes from July 13 and August 3 sessions, payment of bills, budget and investment reports, and donations from Lynn Miller, Nikki O'Neal, and an anonymous donor. The motion was approved, though Bouché acknowledged moving too quickly and noted he heard Vice President Trollop's (participating virtually) vote at the end.

Representatives Chris and Kevin Hickman of Nexus provided updates on construction at John Marshall, Rib Mountain, Franklin, and Lincoln schools, noting occupancy inspections were scheduled for the following week and most classrooms had been turned over for cleaning. Kevin Hickman thanked the district for a 12-year partnership and credited the community-approved referendum with producing 'safer schools, renewed infrastructure, and improving environments.' Board member Pat McKee publicly noted that Nexus president Mike had not appeared before the board since threatening legal action years earlier, calling it a missed opportunity for a 'decent touch,' and asked Hickman to relay that message.

discussions.item: District Class Size Presentation and Discussion
discussions.body: Administration presented current class size guidelines (K-1: max 25; 2-3: max 27; 4-5: max 29; AGR schools K-3: max 18), six years of average class size data showing district average of 20.2 for 2026-27, and modeled an alternative 21-23-25 framework that would require eight additional sections and approximately $1.1 million in staffing costs against a projected $1.36 million budget shortfall for 2027-28. Board members engaged in extensive debate: Pat McKee argued for a 'classroom complexity factor' beyond pure enrollment numbers, drawing applause; Lance Trollop (virtual) pushed back on media framing that class sizes had hit a six-year high, noting the increase was less than one student; Cory Sillars advocated for adding para support to younger grades and requested a school-by-school staffing model; Jennifer Paoli asked about para allocation processes and whether a lower-cost para increase could substitute for new sections; and Nick Crochiere raised the possibility of a future referendum targeted at class size reduction. Administration confirmed Rib Mountain first grade would receive an enrollment para given its enrollment at the maximum, and noted the district is already approximately 40 staff short with two weeks until school starts.

District administrator Tabitha Gundrum (identified as Ms. Gundrum/Mensley in transcript) walked the board through eight updated or new policies required by Wisconsin Act 89, passed in March 2026, covering staff-student communication standards, annual training requirements, and mandatory reporting timelines. Key changes include a statutory prohibition on direct staff-to-student personal device communication, with SportsYou and Google Chat identified as approved platforms; removal of 'preferential treatment' language from policies as unenforceable; new 'grooming' definition sections; and strict reporting deadlines requiring parent notification by 5:00 p.m. the same day if a report is received before end of school day, or by noon the next calendar day if received after hours. Gundrum noted training launched August 1 with a 25-minute attorney-produced video, with roughly 30% of staff already completing it, and that volunteer training remains a significant logistical challenge. The board voted unanimously to approve all eight policy changes.

overview: The Village of Kronenwetter's CLIPP Committee met on August 3, 2026, taking action on four items: approving July meeting minutes, recommending the county maintain a four-way stop at County Highway XX and Teraboni Drive, rescinding the Oak Wilt ordinance and reimbursement policy, and recommending a one-year moratorium on data center development to the Village Board. discussions.body: Minutes were moved and seconded with no discussion. The committee approved them 4-0.

The police chief reported approximately 800 calls for service in July, noting an anecdotal spike in domestic violence incidents; one arrest resulted in 10 felony and 3 misdemeanor charges with a $50,000 cash bond. The fire chief reported the department was awarded a WPS Rewarding Responders grant to purchase a new thermal imaging camera and noted an ISO audit scheduled for the following day. The public works/utilities director reported ongoing communication with the FBI and EPA regarding cybersecurity threats to municipal water systems nationally, noting some systems had been hacked due to lack of passwords, and stated Kronenwetter has security measures in place. The complaint log showed seven complaints year-to-date, with staff noting the incoming new community development director starting Thursday would help resume normal enforcement activity.

discussions.item: Four-Way Stop at County Highway XX and Teraboni Drive
discussions.body: Greg presented an email from Marathon County indicating the county's traffic study supports retaining a four-way stop at the intersection, though the county wanted the village's input before a Thursday committee meeting. One committee member noted personal daily use of the intersection and observed it was 'much better' as a four-way stop. The committee voted 4-0 to recommend to the county that the four-way stop be retained, with the understanding that the county retains jurisdiction and makes the final decision.

discussions.item: Oak Wilt Ordinance Review and Rescission
discussions.body: Greg presented proposed changes to the village's Oak Wilt ordinance, noting the village has no tree inspector on staff or under contract, no longer has grant funding to assist residents with removal costs, and that Oak Wilt has spread so widely across Wisconsin that strict local enforcement is impractical. The committee debated village liability and discussed whether maintaining an unenforceable ordinance created risk. The consensus was that without the funding mechanism or tree inspector, the ordinance and associated reimbursement policy should be rescinded, with residents referred to the DNR. The committee voted 4-0 to rescind both the Oak Wilt ordinance and the reimbursement policy.

A committee member introduced the resolution, describing concerns about the massive scale of data centers, their extraordinary water consumption, and the village's existing water capacity challenges. Jim noted he had spoken with a director at Wausau/Marathon County who is developing ordinance language to define and restrict data centers, and offered to share that language with relevant boards. One member noted AI data centers generate strong community opposition. A minor drafting error was caught — the resolution referred to 'the cities' rather than 'the village' — which staff agreed to correct. The committee voted 4-0 to recommend the moratorium resolution directly to the Village Board for approval.

Greg reported that a minimum cost estimate for a new trail in Kronenwetter would be at least $600,000 for construction alone, not including wetlands, culverts, or engineering. The county indicated it would not contribute financially. The committee generally agreed that trail planning should be referred to the Parks Committee for prioritization, and that trail construction is likely most cost-effective when bundled with road projects rather than as standalone projects. A member with prior experience at the Village of Weston noted that trail paths along county roads in that area were historically funded by county and state dollars, not village funds, suggesting a similar approach could apply here if a future connector road is built.

Finance Director John presented the village's first-ever 10-year Capital Improvement Program, noting the village had previously operated entirely year-to-year with no long-term capital plan. The current draft covers approximately $4.3 million in priority projects across departments, with roughly $1.2 million remaining from a 2024 general obligation borrowing and a possible new GO borrowing of approximately $1.7 million. Major infrastructure items include Maple Ridge Road engineering and reconstruction, Martin Road reconstruction (flagged by a committee member as the village's worst road and priority given heavy resident use of the compost site), sewer lift station panel upgrades and SCADA system, a new water tower and well, and deferred municipal center maintenance including boiler and roofing. The fire department noted rescue truck number 6 would need to be ordered well before its 2029 scheduled replacement due to 3-4 year delivery timelines. The document was presented as a living, versioned working document to be refined through August, September, and October ahead of November budget adoption.

No other members of the public spoke.

overview: The Village of Weston Community Development Authority held a brief meeting on the closing of TIF District No. 1, which added $354 million in assessed value since 1998 and accumulated $95.7 million in increment over its life. The CDA voted unanimously to redeem the outstanding 2017A lease revenue bonds early, paying off debt ahead of the 2031 schedule. The board also received an update on TIF District No. 2, which carries a $841,000 deficit and is expected to close within a few years, and discussed the future role of the CDA itself.

discussions.body: A motion to approve the minutes was made by Lisa and seconded by Ted. The motion passed unanimously with no discussion.

Staff (identified as Jessica) reported that TIF District No. 1, open since 1998, has recovered all costs and is ready to close. The TIF added $354 million in assessed value, incurred $86 million in project costs, and collected $95.7 million in total increment. Members asked whether sufficient funds exist to call the outstanding debt; Jessica confirmed they do. Staff noted that closing the TIF will shift the assessed value to the general tax roll, likely producing a significant tax rate reduction for village residents, and that the village expects to be allowed to increase its levy by approximately $400,000. Approximately $200,000 in administration cost allocations will also return to the general fund.

Jessica reported that TIF District No. 2, created in 2004 around Schofield Avenue, carries a $841,000 deficit following a large state-mandated value reduction last year. The TIF has no remaining debt, only the deficit to repay through ongoing increment. No new projects or expenditures are planned; the district is expected to close before its 2031 deadline. Members also briefly discussed the possibility of future TIFs, including a potential small district near Highway J, but staff noted no formal proposal exists and that changes to state TIF law are still evolving.

discussions.body: The board voted on a resolution to call and redeem the outstanding CDA lease revenue bonds (Series 2017A, dated July 13, 2017), paying bondholders in full with interest rather than continuing payments through 2031. A member identified as Hogan moved approval and Mark seconded. The motion passed unanimously.

Members and staff discussed whether the CDA should continue to exist once TIF 2 closes, noting it has no debt to administer and has not conducted business visits since 2018. Staff suggested bringing the question of disbanding or repurposing the CDA to the full Village Board for direction, and a member asked staff to add it to the board's next monthly agenda. Members noted the CDA is established by ordinance, so any dissolution would require a formal ordinance change.

discussions.body: Keefe Wolkowski spoke in favor of the zero-lot line concept, noting he first brought it to the Planning Commission about two years ago. He explained that the proposal involves 60-foot-wide lots that would allow twin-home ownership, with each owner holding their half, and cited adoption by Rothschild, Weston, and Marshfield. He noted Gary Gurn and Timberidge Builders are interested in a mixed twin-home and single-family development in Kronenwetter.

Resident Guy Fredel made an extended argument for keeping the Quasquerot interchange in the Wausau MPO's long-range transportation plan, noting that Duane Gaau (MPO chairperson) had written to President Joling asking for the village's position. Fredel highlighted that federal interchange standards have been reduced from seven criteria to two, that state law requires Wisconsin to cover 100% of costs if a federal waiver is needed, and that two state representatives had expressed interest in funding it in the next budget cycle. He argued safety concerns on the current I-39 northbound ramp support the interchange.

Finance Director John James reported the village is at roughly 54% of revenues collected and 43% of expenditures spent at the six-month mark, which he characterized as healthy overall. He flagged three areas of concern: the village attorney budget is $10,000 over budget due to a personnel investigation with more invoices expected; the municipal building is at 53% spent due to unexpected repairs from deferred maintenance; and the garbage/recycling budget is at 54% spent due to a diesel fuel surcharge triggered when prices exceed $4 per contract. James indicated the $60,000 contingency reserve would be used to address overages via future budget amendments through APC and the board.

Finance Director James presented a timetable calling for the CIP budget review to begin at the August 3rd CLIP committee meeting, with two budget workshops planned for October 19 and 20, with the October 19 meeting starting earlier in the afternoon to avoid conflicting with Planning Commission. Final budget adoption is targeted for the November 9 board meeting. Trustees were encouraged to attend any committee budget meetings and to raise questions early so the final adoption meeting would be largely settled.

Marathon County Highway Commissioner Kevin Lee clarified that the facility's water plan involves three components: the main building connected to village sewer and water, a private well for brine-making (a high-volume use that does not enter the sewer), and a private well for the wash bay with metered sewer discharge. The board approved the rezoning 7-0.

Multiple trustees expressed support, with one noting the previous failure was partly due to misperceptions that these would be low-income rentals, when in fact units sell for approximately $400,000 per side. The board reached consensus to direct staff and the Planning Commission to gather ordinances from neighboring communities and draft language for a public hearing and future board approval. discussions.body: Mishka reported the village was awarded a $5,000 grant from the Wausau Marathon County Parks and Recreation Foundation, with the foundation expressing a preference (not a requirement) for a $5,000 municipal match. Finance Director James said the match would be moved from the existing general fund parks budget into a dedicated park fund for transparency, with a formal budget amendment to come through APC in August. The board approved the $5,000 match 7-0, with trustees noting that matching demonstrates community investment and positions the village well for future grant applications.

The amendment adds the cost to the capital projects fund. Trustee Lesniak moved and Trustee Solheim seconded; the board approved 7-0.

title: Environmental Resources Committee - Educational Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Environmental Resources Committee held a special educational meeting with no votes taken, featuring conservation staff introductions and program updates, followed by background on proposed animal waste ordinance changes. Four public commenters addressed concerns about manure spreading regulations, wind turbine development, and water quality, while staff presented on municipal wellhead protection successes in Athens and Rib Mountain, a walleye telemetry study on the Big Eau Pleine, and shoreline restoration projects.

discussions.item: Public Comment - Manure Ordinance and Agriculture Regulations
discussions.body: Christine Cafer (Town of McMillan) questioned where the other 72% of phosphorus load in the Wisconsin River basin originates beyond Marathon County's 28%, raised concerns about storage cost burdens on farms without facilities, and asked the committee to identify scientific evidence that additional county regulations will produce measurable improvements beyond existing state programs. Dean Beck, a member of the animal waste task force representing eastern Marathon County, warned that the proposed ordinance focuses only on animal waste while commercial fertilizer used by crop farmers contains equally significant phosphorus and nitrogen, potentially undermining the ordinance's water quality goals. Pat Saha (Town of Repro), also on the task force, expressed general support for a February-March winter spreading ban and for requiring nutrient management plans for all farmers, and shared a positive personal experience installing buffer strips that improved water quality without reducing yield.

discussions.item: Public Comment - Hub City Wind and Utility-Scale Wind Development
discussions.body: Nikki Catrell (Town of Brighton) asked the committee to place utility-scale wind development on a future agenda and to recommend the county board adopt a temporary moratorium while evaluating whether current ordinances adequately address projects of this scale. She argued that modern turbines are dramatically larger than those that shaped existing regulations and cited a Wisconsin Badger Hollow Wind proceeding in which independent audiologist Dr. Jerry Punch from Michigan State University found a developer's acoustic analysis fundamentally inadequate, concluding that independent expert review is necessary before irreversible decisions are made. She drew a parallel to the committee's planned August consideration of a moratorium on data centers, arguing the same principle should apply to wind development.

discussions.item: Conservation Staff Introductions and Program Overview
discussions.body: Conservation staff — Matt Reking, Ken Pazorski (who announced his retirement after 35 years), Kirk Lane, Brooke Benick, Caleb Armstrong, and Jared Mdd — each described their program areas including animal waste ordinance administration, livestock licensing, farmland preservation, nutrient management training, managed grazing, the EPIC producer group, youth education, and water resources. Staff noted the team has over 130 combined years of experience across eight conservationists. A committee member asked about anaerobic digesters, and staff clarified that digesters in Marathon County are all on CAFO farms regulated by the state DNR, so the county is not directly involved.

discussions.item: Wisconsin Land and Water Training Debrief
discussions.body: Staff invited committee members to share takeaways from a Wisconsin Land and Water training held in Merrill approximately six weeks prior. One committee member highlighted learning about Lincoln County's culvert fish passage assessment and the technical complexity of manure spill response. Staff noted that Marathon County statistically has the fifth most manure spills in Wisconsin. The session was informal and conversational, with no formal action.

discussions.item: Municipal Wellhead Protection Updates - Athens, Rib Mountain, Hatley
discussions.body: Staff described the completed Athens project, where 30 acres nearest municipal wells were converted to prairie and 30 acres to pasture, eliminating row-crop nutrient applications near wells with increasing nitrates. The private landowner received a higher rental payment than under row crops. Staff reported Athens residents have embraced the prairie on social media and the village reached out this week requesting more prairie. A similar project is underway in Rib Mountain adjacent to Rib Mountain State Park and Depkey Park on County Road N, with multiple funding sources stacked to make the project a win for all parties. Staff also reported early-stage outreach to the Village of Hatley, which has only one municipal well with nitrates already above 7 mg/L and rising, serving a population of about 500 with an average age of 33.

discussions.item: Big Eau Pleine Walleye Acoustic Telemetry Fish Movement Study
discussions.body: Jared Mdd presented updates on a 10-year walleye tagging study initiated through a surface water grant that also funded replacement of the Big Eau Pleine aeration system (originally installed in 1980). In year one, 30 walleye were tagged; 8 were caught by anglers, 7 were harvested but all tags returned and recycled. In year two, 12 additional tags were purchased and 7 new fish tagged. Receivers are placed throughout the flowage to track fish movement every 30 seconds via acoustic pings. Staff noted 4 receivers are currently missing, likely lost during spring ice breakup, and DNR divers will search for them this fall. One fish passed through Moon Dam and is believed to be in Lake Dubay.

discussions.item: Animal Waste Ordinance Proposed Changes Overview
discussions.body: Staff briefly reviewed proposed ordinance changes that have been under discussion for approximately eight months to a year, given time constraints. Key proposals include: requiring a nutrient management plan or a winter spreading permit for anyone applying liquid manure in winter, with setbacks from water bodies and sensitive areas; and a February-March liquid manure spreading ban for farms at approximately 300 animal units (roughly 150 milk cows and 150 young stock) or greater. CAFO operations at 1,000 animal units or greater are already subject to these requirements under state law. Staff noted the animal waste ordinance work group of approximately 25 stakeholders — including farmers, water resource professionals, and seed dealers — has been involved in developing these proposals. The meeting ended before a full discussion could occur due to time constraints.

publicComment: Four speakers offered public comment. Christine Cafer (Town of McMillan) raised concerns about the cost burden of manure storage facilities, questioned the scientific basis for county regulations beyond existing state programs, and asked where the other 72% of Wisconsin River phosphorus load originates. Nikki Catrell (Town of Brighton) requested the committee place utility-scale wind development on a future agenda and consider a temporary moratorium, citing concerns about outdated ordinances and the need for independent acoustic review, analogous to the planned data center moratorium. Dean Beck (County East), a member of the animal waste task force, warned that excluding crop farmers using commercial fertilizer from the ordinance would undermine phosphorus reduction goals. Pat Saha (Town of Repro), also on the task force, expressed support for the February-March winter spreading ban, mandatory nutrient management plans, and buffer strips, sharing a positive personal experience with buffers on his own farm.

discussions.body: One member of the public, Jim, spoke on three topics: opposition to removing the legal detail from Finance and HR Committee packets, requesting to comment during the Cintas contract discussion given his two decades of experience with uniform contracts, and criticizing the exit interview report for including staff opinions rather than factual employee interview data. discussions.item: June Budget Status Report and TIF Reports (Items 5-7)
discussions.body: A committee member asked Finance Director Jessica about the aquatic center revenue covering 50.42% of expenditures to date, and Jessica explained season pass sales in June account for a large portion of revenue. She noted the aquatic center receives $40,000 in property tax levy and $40,000 in room tax annually, and that balancing it is a year-to-year struggle. Items 5, 6, and 7 were acknowledged together by motion.

Staff reported three transitions in the past six months. It was noted that a previously full-time deputy clerk position was split into two part-time positions successfully, reducing benefit costs. An engineering tech (RAS) was recently brought on, and two positions — deputy clerk/administrative assistant and utility operator/maintainer — were currently posted for recruitment.

HR staff Jamie presented the report, noting only one exit interview was completed and that for confidentiality reasons no specific recommendations were attributed to that individual. The report included commentary about increasing negativity and unconstructive criticism affecting staff morale, which generated significant discussion. A committee member argued the win of a 7.5% turnover rate — below public sector benchmarks — was being overshadowed by the opinion-laden portion of the report and suggested separating the factual turnover data from the morale discussion, making the latter a standing agenda item. Mark (identified in discussion as a village official present) stated he personally refuses to respond to criticism in outside media and expressed support for staff. A department director spoke about the difficulty staff face being identified in public while wearing village shirts and receiving negative comments. Jamie defended including the morale content as reflective of themes heard more broadly, not just from the one exit interview, noting it could be a leading indicator if turnover worsens. The committee agreed to add a standing item for August on how the committee can better support staff, and one member proposed adding encomiums as a standing agenda item at board meetings. The motion to acknowledge the report passed with one opposed vote.

Public commenter Jim, who was invited to speak, shared detailed experience with uniform contracts, recommending the village negotiate seasonal garment rates to avoid makeup charges, standardize garment types to reduce costs (noting stretchy jeans cost four times standard pants), and consider an allowance model where employees pay the difference for premium options. DPW Director Michael explained the current contract uses Omnia Partners government pricing locking rates for 36 months, that Cintas would not go below a 36-month term, and that a minimum weekly charge of approximately $45 (50% of current ~$92/week bill) would still be met even if some employees opted out. He noted communication and weekly check-ins with the Cintas driver have improved. The committee discussed the opt-out hybrid model, employee satisfaction, female employees having difficulty finding well-fitting garments, and the January 1 start date for annual selections. The committee recommended approval of the Cintas uniform agreement renewal to the board of trustees.

The committee discussed amendments to Chapter 5 (job classification and compensation, clothing and equipment loans) and Chapter 10 (appearance) of the personnel policies handbook to reflect the new hybrid uniform program — allowing employees to either use Cintas or receive a $500 clothing allowance, compared to the current $300 reimbursement. Staff confirmed this was essentially codifying the agreement approved in Item 10. The committee recommended approval of the policy amendments to the board of trustees.

Finance Director Jessica presented a proposal from Hawkins Ash to continue as the village's auditor for the 2026 audit at a cost of $41,105. She noted this is lower than the $43,000–$46,000 proposals received from other firms during the last RFP process (for the 2025 audit), and that retaining Hawkins Ash is beneficial because of their familiarity with the village's TIF districts and existing work papers. The committee recommended approval of the one-year extension to the board of trustees.

Finance Director Jessica presented the final 2025 audit report from Hawkins Ash, noting she had included a memo summarizing the highlights to make the voluminous document more accessible. A committee member appreciated the memo. The committee acknowledged the final audit report without significant discussion.

Finance Director Amy (or Jessica) presented a proposed budget calendar, noting that the September 7 meeting date falls on Labor Day and should be moved to Tuesday, September 8. The committee discussed whether Finance and HR should hold joint meetings with the full board of trustees throughout the budget process or focus narrowly on wages and benefits as in prior years. Two committee members expressed preference for participating in the full budget process. The motion to approve the calendar and hold joint meetings with the board was approved unanimously.

discussions.body: The chair introduced this item, explaining that after raising the concept at the last board of trustees meeting, the board referred the task of developing a potential ethics process to the Finance and HR Committee. The chair noted the current ethics policy (page 226 of the packet) routes violations to a department director or administrator, and that the committee would explore whether to build upon, amend, or replace it. A committee member suggested a citizen-based body similar to the police and fire commission, with the chair agreeing that was a possibility worth considering. The chair noted the committee may grow from four to six members after that evening's board of trustees meeting and wanted to wait for that input before going deeper. Staff were asked to gather sample ethics policies from comparable municipalities for the August meeting discussion.

He also drew on his 20-plus years of experience with Cintas and uniform contracts to request time to speak during the Cintas agenda item, which was granted. Finally, he criticized the exit interview report for including staff opinions rather than factual interview data and suggested the committee hold a listening session for staff to share thoughts directly.

overview: The Weston Village Board of Trustees held a wide-ranging meeting covering several significant decisions, most notably approving the Mountain Bay Metropolitan Police Department building contract with 8 Pine Inc. for $6.7 million — coming in under a $7 million budget — and receiving a detailed presentation from DC Everest school district leaders on long-range facility planning that could include a $81–94 million referendum in April 2027. discussions.item: DC Everest Long-Range Facility Planning Presentation
discussions.body: Superintendent Dr. Casey Nye and Assistant Superintendent Dr. Kelly Strike presented DC Everest's long-range facility plan, which involves decommissioning the 75-year-old junior high, moving 8th graders to the middle school (creating a 6–8 building) and 9th graders to the high school (creating a 9–12 building), with an estimated cost of $81–94 million plus potential additional costs if a new aquatics facility is added. The district is targeting an April 2027 referendum, noting that current enrollment has declined from about 5,900 five years ago to 5,730, and that the 2018 referendum passed with roughly 70.8% approval. Trustees asked about the operational costs of retaining the junior high structure partially, staffing reductions (attrition-based, no planned layoffs), the age of other facilities, and the potential pool project near GTCC. Dr. Nye acknowledged the pool decision is exploratory and that community partnership conversations are ongoing.

discussions.item: Mountain Bay Metro Police Department Bid Results (Item 54)
discussions.body: Chief Mark Kern presented bid results for the new Mountain Bay Metropolitan Police Department building: the base bid from contractor 8 Pine Inc. came in at $6,390,100, with the total project including fiber optic line, lockers, furniture, and security estimated at $6.7 million — under the $7 million budget. Five bid alternatives were considered; three were eliminated. The approximately 26,000 sq. ft. building includes a 13-squad garage expandable during adverse weather. Trustee Katrina Clark expressed disappointment at the process that led to needing a new building, saying she felt misled when the merger was approved after being told existing facilities were adequate; Chief Kern took personal responsibility, apologizing to the board. Finance administrator Ryan noted an intergovernmental agreement with Rothschild must be finalized in August before the contract with 8 Pine can be signed; 8 Pine indicated it could begin construction by end of September. Weston's share is approximately $4,355,000 (65%), with Rothschild covering 35%. The board voted unanimously 7-0 to approve the contract.

Trustee Barbara Ermeling reported the committee discussed the Cintas agreement and an annual exit interview report showing 7.5% village-wide staff turnover, which she characterized as a strong result for a public entity. The committee also discussed ways elected officials can show appreciation to staff, with follow-up planned for August.

Director Michael reported the Alderson-Gelnik roundabout is progressing with curb and gutter poured and sidewalk work beginning; utility pole removal was delayed until after the World Cup finale due to telecom contract restrictions. A utility operator gave two-week notice — the third consecutive year of turnover in that position around the one-year mark — raising concerns about operational impact and training burden. Discussion also covered the asbestos pipe replacement program (10 miles in the village, with a grant being pursued), street lighting gaps near the river and along Score Avenue to campus, and the long-term future of the bridge over the Oclair River on Ross Avenue. Trustees also discussed the planned Ross Avenue and Camp Phillips roundabout, driven by crash analysis and a traffic study showing the intersection trending toward level-of-service F by 2034.

Village President Maloney and others briefly discussed the SAFER board's approval of adding three staff for 2027, which the board indicated they have comfort funding via TIF district closure revenue without a referendum. Maloney expressed the need for a longer-term staffing plan — potentially adding two more in year two and three more in year three — to be discussed during budget season, noting the public's rejection of the fire fee referendum signaled they do not want another referendum approach.

discussions.item: Bushka Park Renovation Project Grant Update
discussions.body: Staff reported that three grants were submitted, including one to WASOW (outcome pending) and the Marathon County Parks and Recreation Foundation Fund grant for which the village received $5,000. A committee member asked for clarification on whether $100,000 was the total grant pool or the eligibility cap. Staff noted they had a call in with WASOW and expected to hear back. A motion was made by Patty and seconded by another member to recommend the village board approve a $5,000 match to the received grant; the motion carried 7-0.

The committee conducted a lengthy park-by-park review of Municipal Park, Towering Pines, Friendship Park, Bushka Park, and Seville Park. Recurring themes across all parks included failing ADA accessibility (notably only one handicap swing in the village, which is itself inaccessible), aging playground equipment (15-20 years old), vandalism of bathrooms, poorly maintained Little Free Libraries, signage issues, and underuse of facilities. Staff member Greg confirmed budget constraints with only three part-time parks staff and five full-time streets staff covering seven parks. The committee directed staff to compile a prioritized list with rough cost estimates for the next meeting, and noted that a full assessment cannot be completed until all parks are reviewed. ADA compliance was identified as a high-priority cross-park issue.

discussions.item: August 21, 2026 Concert at Towering Pines Fundraiser Event
discussions.body: Committee member Patty presented a plan for a fundraiser concert featuring donated band Living River on August 21, with proposed amenities including a bounce house, petting zoo, face painting, and free food funded by a $2,000 village board allocation from the community events budget. Trustees Mishka and Lesniak expressed concern about using village funds for a fundraising event with uncertain returns, and about event redundancy given National Night Out and the planned 5K. A motion by Patty for up to $2,000 from the village board was seconded for discussion purposes; the motion failed with only Patty voting yes. Following the failed vote, Patty indicated she would cancel the August 21 event and look at rescheduling to spring 2027.

Committee member Aaron presented a detailed plan for a 5K/3K run-walk starting at Bushka Park, passing through Towering Pines, and ending at Relocation Public Eatery, with music provided by a musician personally sponsored by Village President Dan Joling. Police Chief Terry McEwen confirmed police support for road closures. Relocation owner Jackie Fisher approved the event and proposed raffle baskets, 50/50 drawings, and potentially donating a percentage of food and drink sales. The committee discussed shirt pricing (roughly $9-$13 per shirt), registration fees ($25 per person or $50 per family discussed), and a shirt deadline for early registrants. A motion to recommend the village board approve this as an official village event passed unanimously 7-0.

discussions.item: Creating a Friends of Kronenwetter Parks Support Group
discussions.body: Chair Mishka distributed a handout outlining steps to establish a Friends of Kronenwetter Parks nonprofit support group. The committee agreed by consensus to table detailed discussion and review the materials before the next meeting, with no vote taken.

Committee members proposed four future agenda items: Norm Plaza Park for a possible dog park, a disc golf course at the wellhead park (larger than Seville), water access points along the river for kayak and canoe landings, and placement of benches along walking trails. Additional future items suggested included further 5K planning details and a discussion of a 2027 village events calendar.

discussions.item: FEMA Declaration and Community Assistance Update
discussions.body: Sarah, the county's Public Information Officer, presented a detailed update on FEMA and SBA disaster assistance following the April 13–23, 2026 severe storms, tornadoes, and flooding. She reported that as of July 15, 24 Marathon County residents had filed FEMA individual assistance applications, with four filed the previous day. A FEMA Disaster Recovery Center opened July 14 at the Town of Ringle Municipal Center (Monday–Friday, 1–7 p.m.), and an SBA Business Recovery Center opened July 13 at the Marathon County Public Library Wausau headquarters (Monday–Friday, 9 a.m.–4:30 p.m.). A new recovery resource page was also launched at marathoncounty.gov/ia.

Sarah explained that while Marathon County was approved for individual assistance, it was denied for FEMA public assistance — which covers governmental costs such as debris removal, road repairs, and public infrastructure — along with Bayfield, Manitowoc, and Racine counties. The per-capita damage threshold for Marathon County was $670,743.18, but documented damages from the April storms totaled only approximately $271,000. County staff reviewed whether any additional damages had been missed and concluded they had not; therefore, the county informed Wisconsin Emergency Management it would not pursue an appeal. Gibbs emphasized to committee members that the public assistance denial does not affect individuals' ability to apply for individual assistance.

discussions.item: Insurance Settlements and Town of Ringle Property Questions
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson asked about the status of insurance company settlements for homes in the Town of Ringle that may need to be demolished, raising concerns about deadlines and potential need for the county to extend deadlines or forgive fees. Gibbs responded that he had not received a follow-up from Ringle representatives but pledged to reach out, noting that Sarah had attended a recent Ringle board meeting on these topics. He mentioned that free legal consultation through the State Bar of Wisconsin and resources from the State Commission on Insurance had been made available to affected residents, and that the Town of Ringle was also exploring whether to issue raze orders for disputed properties.

Gibbs presented the item on behalf of Vice Chair Boots, who had to leave to catch a flight. He asked committee members whether anything was missing from the strategic plan survey included in their packets. Supervisor Arseth asked whether the survey would be available online; Gibbs confirmed it would be sent to county board members as a link-based online survey, similar to the work plan ranking process. No content gaps were identified by members present. Gibbs noted a separate public input process would be used.

discussions.body: The board discussed three options for handling election-related ordinance revisions stemming from five complaints filed during the 2024 election: (A) adopt the CLIP-drafted language, (B) rely on existing state statutes and corrective actions already taken, or (C) work with the attorney to refine the ordinance. After extended debate about the risks of mirroring state statutes in local ordinance and the need to avoid ongoing maintenance issues, Trustee Coyle withdrew the motion. The board ultimately directed Clerk Jennifer to draft internal policy guidelines incorporating corrective actions and aligned with state statute, then bring the result back to CLIP for review. Clerk Jennifer presented the proposal citing U.S. Postal Service delays causing some residents to miss ballot return deadlines. The board debated the need for surveillance cameras on the box; it was ultimately agreed that a camera would not be installed initially. The motion was then amended by Trustee Stowell to include both the August primary and November general election, with a report back to the board on usage and any damage. overview: The Village of Weston Public Works Committee met on July 13, 2026, covering active construction project updates, utility operations, and two action items: awarding a surveying contract for Howland Avenue and awarding the Concord Avenue/Bayberry Street reconstruction bid to HS Suns. The committee also held an extended discussion on future capital needs including the aging Ross Avenue bridge over the Eau Claire River, street lighting gaps, PFAS treatment, and asbestos cement water main replacement.
